content.title: About
content.content: Baby Toddler Yogurt with Fruit is a gentle dairy product specially formulated for children aged 6 months to 3 years. It contains whole milk, live probiotic cultures, and natural fruit puree, without added sugar or artificial flavors.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The yogurt contains live Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium cultures that support a healthy gut microbiome in toddlers.
Fruit puree is made from 100 % fresh fruits with no added sugars.
The product meets strict quality standards and complies with the national regulations for infant nutrition.
Its smooth, creamy texture is easy for little hands to handle independently.
Packaging is made from safe, reusable plastic suitable for young children.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Probiotics promote the growth of beneficial gut bacteria, improving digestion and reducing the risk of constipation.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: The dairy base provides a high level of calcium essential for bone and teeth development.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Yogurt supplies vitamin B2 (riboflavin) and vitamin B12, important for energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Natural fruit antioxidants
items.content: Fruit puree adds vitamin C and polyphenols that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: Low lactose content and soft texture make it suitable even for children with mild lactose intolerance.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Children allergic to cow’s milk may react to this product; an alternative dairy‑free option should be used.

items.title: Natural fruit sugars
items.content: Although no sugar is added, natural sugars from the fruit puree can affect blood glucose in children with diabetes.

items.title: Storage after opening
items.content: Once opened, keep the container refrigerated and consume within 48 hours to prevent spoilage.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the yogurt as a standalone snack, stir into baby cereals, mix with purees, or use as a filling for mini pancakes. Before serving, gently stir to evenly distribute the fruit puree.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator at 2‑6 °C. Do not freeze. After opening, keep in a sealed container and use within 48 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Greens are leafy vegetables such as spinach, kale, Swiss chard and others that can be eaten raw or lightly cooked with added fat. Cooking preserves most vitamins, and a small amount of oil enhances the absorption of fat‑soluble nutrients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Leafy vegetables are rich in chlorophyll, giving them a vivid green color and antioxidant properties.
Heat treatment breaks down some cell walls, making nutrients more bioavailable.
Adding fat (oil) increases the bioavailability of vitamins A, D, E and K found in greens.
Fresh greens are commonly used in salads, while cooked greens appear in soups, stews and side dishes.
Some greens, like spinach, contain oxalates that can bind calcium.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Greens provide folate (B9), vitamin B6 and other B‑vitamins important for metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Source of vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Lutein, zeaxanthin and other carotenoids protect the eyes from age‑related changes.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber in greens promotes intestinal motility and a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Aids weight control
items.content: Low calorie density and high water content make greens filling without excess calories.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Certain greens (e.g., spinach, rhubarb) contain oxalates that may contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: Fresh greens are often treated with pesticides; thorough washing before consumption is recommended.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Rarely, some people may be allergic to specific leafy vegetables.

items.title: Overcooking
items.content: Prolonged cooking can degrade heat‑sensitive vitamins, especially vitamin C.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Add fresh greens to salads, smoothies and sandwiches. Cooked greens can be sautéed with a small amount of olive or butter, used in soups, omelets or as a side dish for meats.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh greens in the refrigerator in a perforated bag with a slight moisture to keep them crisp for up to 5 days. Cooked greens should be kept in an airtight container in the fridge and consumed within 3 days.

hamburger-on-wheat-bun-1-small-patty.title: Hamburger on wheat bun, 1 small patty

content.title: About
content.content: A hamburger on a wheat bun with one small beef patty (1701) is a classic fast‑food item consisting of a soft bun, juicy patty, lettuce leaf, tomato slice, pickles and sauce. It is often served with fries and a drink.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first hamburger was served in the United States in the late 19th century.
A wheat bun gives a softer texture compared with traditional rye buns.
The patty weighs about 50 g, making it “small” compared with standard burger patties.
The hamburger is a symbol of American culture and is popular worldwide.
There are countless topping variations: cheese, bacon, avocado, various sauces.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: The beef patty provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Red meat is rich in heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Hamburgers contain vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Carbohydrates for energy
items.content: The wheat bun supplies complex carbohydrates that give lasting satiety.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: If the bun is whole‑grain, it adds fiber that benefits digestion.

items.title: High fat and calorie content
items.content: A hamburger can be calorie‑dense and contain saturated fats, so it should be eaten in moderation.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Sauces and processed ingredients may increase salt intake, which is undesirable for hypertension.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The wheat bun contains gluten, which can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked patty may harbor pathogens such as E. coli.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Hamburgers are typically eaten by hand, holding them with both hands. Add cheese, bacon, sauces, and fresh vegetables to suit your taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store a prepared hamburger in the refrigerator for no more than 24 hours in an airtight container. For longer storage, separate the components: the bun can be frozen, and the patty can be kept in the freezer for up to 3 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Kidney beans are large, meaty beans with a bright red color, belonging to the species Phaseolus vulgaris. They are widely used in many cuisines, especially in tomato‑based dishes, chili, salads, and stews. The beans are rich in protein, complex carbohydrates, and dietary fiber.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name "kidney" comes from the bean’s shape, which resembles a human kidney.
More than 30 varieties of kidney beans exist, differing in size and shade of red.
Raw beans contain phytohemagglutinin, a toxic protein that is destroyed by proper cooking.
In the United States, kidney beans are a staple ingredient in chili con carne.
Soaking beans overnight speeds up cooking and improves nutrient absorption.

items.title: Rich source of plant protein
items.content: One cup of cooked kidney beans provides about 15 g of protein, making it valuable for vegetarians and vegans.

items.title: High dietary fiber content
items.content: Fiber supports healthy digestion and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains iron and folate
items.content: These micronutrients are essential for blood formation and anemia prevention, especially in women of childbearing age.

items.title: Low glycemic index after cooking
items.content: Cooked beans raise blood glucose slowly, which is beneficial for people with diabetes.

items.title: Antioxidant compounds
items.content: Kidney beans contain polyphenols that help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Toxicity of raw beans
items.content: Raw kidney beans contain phytohemagglutinin, which can cause severe food poisoning. Cook beans at a rolling boil for at least 10 minutes to destroy the toxin.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Beans may cause flatulence due to oligosaccharides; soaking and discarding the soaking water can reduce this effect.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to legumes.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Kidney beans are best enjoyed after boiling or stewing. Add them to chili, stews, salads, soups, or blend into a bean dip. They can also replace chickpeas in hummus recipes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry beans in an airtight container in a cool, dry place for up to 1 year. Cooked beans keep in the refrigerator for 4‑5 days or can be frozen in portion‑size bags.

content.title: About
content.content: Carnation Instant Breakfast is a ready‑to‑drink powdered breakfast mix that provides milk protein, vitamins, and minerals. It dissolves easily in milk or water, creating a nutritious beverage often used as a quick breakfast or snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The product was first launched in the 1950s to meet the growing demand for convenient breakfasts.
Each serving contains about 12 g of protein, making it a good protein source for active individuals.
The formula includes B‑vitamins, vitamin D, and calcium to support bone health and energy.
The powder is lightweight, non‑perishable until opened, and does not require refrigeration.
Carnation Instant Breakfast is frequently used in sports nutrition and recovery programs.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: A single serving provides roughly 12 g of high‑quality milk protein, important for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of vitamins and minerals
items.content: Enriched with vitamins A, C, D, E, B‑complex, as well as calcium and iron, supporting immunity and bone health.

items.title: Convenient and fast to prepare
items.content: The powder dissolves in liquid within 30‑60 seconds, saving time in the morning or on the go.

items.title: Energy support
items.content: Contains carbohydrates and vitamin B12, helping to boost energy levels and concentration.

items.title: Suitable for children and adults
items.content: Mild flavor and balanced nutrition make it a common choice for kids and seniors alike.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: The product contains dairy protein and may trigger reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk allergy.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Some varieties contain added sugar, which may be unsuitable for diabetics or those watching their sugar intake.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: One serving provides about 200 kcal, so it should be accounted for in total daily calories.

items.title: Artificial flavors
items.content: Certain versions may include artificial flavors or sweeteners that some consumers prefer to avoid.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Mix one serving (≈30 g) with 200‑250 ml of milk, water, or a plant‑based beverage, stir with a whisk or shake in a bottle. Add fruit, nuts, or honey for extra flavor if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the package in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep the bag tightly sealed to prevent moisture ingress.

content.title: About
content.content: White confectioners' sugar (powdered sugar) is a finely ground crystalline sugar, often fortified with a small amount of starch to prevent caking. It is widely used in baking, for dusting pastries, and in the preparation of icings, frostings, and desserts.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Powdered sugar gets its name from its fine, powder‑like texture.
About 3 % cornstarch is typically added to prevent clumping.
In the United States it is known as "confectioners' sugar," while in Russia it is called "сахарная пудра."
Its fine texture allows it to dissolve quickly, making it ideal for smooth icings without graininess.
The delicate dusting effect is often used to create a "snowfall" look on cakes.

items.title: Quick source of energy
items.content: Sugar is rapidly absorbed, providing an immediate boost of glucose to the bloodstream.

items.title: Flavor enhancement
items.content: Small amounts of powdered sugar can amplify the perceived sweetness of other ingredients, improving overall taste.

items.title: Blood sugar spikes
items.content: Excessive consumption can lead to hyperglycemia and increase the risk of developing diabetes.

items.title: Dental caries
items.content: Sugar serves as a food source for oral bacteria that cause tooth enamel decay.

items.title: Starch allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be sensitive to the added cornstarch and experience food intolerance.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Powdered sugar is used for dusting baked goods, making icings, frostings, marzipan, and in no‑bake recipes where rapid dissolution is desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store powdered sugar in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Moisture can cause it to cake; if this happens, sift before use.
